claims.statement: For A = {x+i : x <= X}, |r_d| <= 1 for every admissible ideal and this is sharp, so sum_{N(d)<=D}|r_d| ~ D and Type I holds exactly for D = o(X) = o(Q^{1/2}).
The number of admissible Gaussian ideals of norm <= D is ~ (3/2pi) D, the residue of zeta(s)L(s,chi_4)/zeta(2s) at s=1.
d divides x+i if and only if x == r_d (mod N(d)) for a single residue r_d with r_d^2+1 == 0.
For A = {x+i}, the bilinear incidence graph contains no 4-cycle, so G(n1,n2) = #{m : mn1, mn2 in A} <= 1 for n1 != n2. Holds from both sides, in m and in n alike.
Hypothesis (R1) of the asymptotic sieve for primes requires x^{2/3} < D(x) < x.
claims.citation: Friedlander-Iwaniec, Asymptotic sieve for primes, Ann. of Math. 148 (1998), p.1043 (arXiv:math/9811186)

claims.statement: 'for thin sequences A one cannot expect (R) to hold with D(x) > A(x)'.
claims.citation: ASP p.1044

claims.statement: x^{2/3} is the threshold below which the coefficient gamma(n,C) of hypothesis (B) is annihilated: 'd must be quite a bit smaller than N to ensure that mu(d) does not completely neutralize mu(n) ... our hypothesis (B) can be realistic only if D is somewhat larger than x^{2/3+eps}'.
claims.citation: ASP p.1045

claims.statement: The Friedlander-Iwaniec asymptotic sieve as stated cannot be applied to x^2+1: (R1) demands D > x^{2/3} while Type I caps at x^{1/2}, so the admissible range for D is empty.
Heath-Brown's density exponent alpha places the problems at alpha = 1 (Dirichlet), 3/4 (a^2+b^4), 2/3 (x^3+2y^3), and 1/2 (x^2+1).
claims.citation: Heath-Brown, Primes represented by x^3+2y^3, Acta Math. 186 (2001), p.2 of the Oxford ORA preprint

claims.statement: Heath-Brown did not use the asymptotic sieve: 'their condition (R1) is not quite met in our case ... Although it seems possible that Friedlander and Iwaniec's hypothesis (R1) might be relaxed sufficiently for our application, we have chosen instead to present our own version of the sieve argument.'
claims.citation: HB p.3

claims.statement: Heath-Brown's sequence has level of distribution X^{2-eps} for values of size X^3, i.e. x^{2/3-eps} -- short of (R1) by an epsilon.
claims.citation: HB Lemmas 2.1-2.2, p.5

claims.statement: For a^2+b^4 the level of distribution D = x^{3/4-5eps} is achieved, 'apart from the eps, the best that one can hope for'.
claims.citation: Friedlander-Iwaniec, X^2+Y^4 captures its primes, Prop. 3.5, p.962 (arXiv:math/9811185)

claims.statement: FI's Type I gain comes from applying the Davenport-Halberstam large sieve to the points nu/d with nu^2+1 == 0 (mod d), which for moduli in a short interval are spaced by 1/4D rather than 1/D^2.
claims.citation: X2Y4 Lemma 3.2 and surrounding text, p.957
claims.notes: This repo previously guessed the mechanism was Poisson summation in b. That was wrong; corrected in Note D.

claims.statement: FI prove the Type II bound B(x;N) << A(x)(log x)^{4-A} for x^{1/4+eta} < N < x^{1/2}(log x)^{-B}.
Over dyadic splits, max min(D_m, d_n) ~ sqrt(kappa) = |A|/Q^{1/2}. Measured ratio 0.85-0.92 across the family a^2+b^{2k}, k=2..6 (alpha 0.75 down to 0.583), and 1.26 for x^2+1 where sqrt(kappa)=1.
claims.notes: A degree heuristic supported across a one-parameter family, not a theorem. The C4-free lemma is the proved statement in the neighbourhood. A law fitted from finite data, not a theorem: the extrapolation from the measured range to all X is the unsupported step. Bounded from the other side by kappa-necessary-not-sufficient: at fixed density, kappa does not determine the achievable Type II range. Only the direction kappa = 1 => forest is used by Note F.

claims.statement: sum_m |sum_n mu(n) 1[mn in A]| ~ sqrt(MX) for M <= X, saturating at ~|A| for M >= X. Ratio to sqrt(MX) is 0.88-0.93, stable from X = 2e4 to 1e5.
claims.notes: A law fitted from finite data, not a theorem: the extrapolation from the measured range to all X is the unsupported step.

claims.statement: In the window (B1) would require, M in (x^{1/2}, x^{3/4}), the measured bilinear sum shows no saving at all: S_mu/A(x) = 0.93, 1.00, 1.01.
claims.notes: Exact integer computation over the stated finite range; settles that range completely and implies nothing asymptotic. Independent of the fitted sqrt(MX) law: this is a direct exact computation in the window, not a consequence of the extrapolation. (An earlier version listed that dependency and the registry guard rejected it as resting a rigorous claim on a weaker one.)

claims.statement: Inside FI's proved Prop. 4.1 window the harness sees a^2+b^4 drop to S_mu/|A| = 0.16-0.52 while x^2+1 sits at 0.84-1.01; outside it both saturate. Confirms direction, not magnitude: a log-power saving is invisible over one decade.
claims.notes: Exact integer computation over the stated finite range; settles that range completely and implies nothing asymptotic.

claims.statement: Every level-of-distribution result in this literature concerns primes or smooth numbers in arithmetic progressions, where A(x) = x^{1-o(1)}; the best exponent reached is 5/8-eps. x^{7/12-eps} is Maynard (2020), not Iwaniec, whose contribution is the well-factorability of the linear sieve weights.
claims.notes: Corrected: an earlier version of this claim attributed 7/12 to Iwaniec, and justified inadmissibility by 'weights cannot lift a counting bound', which over-reaches -- sparse-moduli and signed-weight estimates evade counting bounds. The sound reason is that ASP's (R) sums absolute values over all squarefree d <= D.
claims.citation: Maynard arXiv:2006.07088 pp.2-3 (BFI 4/7; Maynard 7/12); Pascadi (Lichtman 66/107, Pascadi 5/8); Polymath 8a arXiv:1402.0811 (Zhang 1/2+1/584, Polymath 1/2+7/300)

claims.statement: Iwaniec (1978) proved that irreducible an^2+bn+c with a>0 and c odd takes P_2 values infinitely often, via a lower-bound weighted sieve; this remains the record for x^2+1.
claims.notes: The original is paywalled; statement taken from an MSc exposition (arXiv:1910.02885), so it is second-hand and classed accordingly.

claims.statement: FI's Type I gain for a^2+b^4 comes from Poisson summation in the b variable.
claims.notes: Guessed by this repo, then refuted by reading X2Y4 p.957: the mechanism is a Davenport-Halberstam large sieve over the roots nu of nu^2+1 == 0 (mod d). Kept so it is not silently re-asserted.

claims.statement: The obstruction for x^2+1 is Type I, not Type II, so the bilinear programme is the wrong half.
claims.notes: Asserted in this repo, then withdrawn. ASP p.1045 shows (R1) is precisely the condition that hypothesis (B) is non-vacuous, so the two are one hypothesis and the dichotomy was malformed.

claims.statement: DFI (Ann. of Math. 141 (1995), 423-441) sec.6 is 'Combinatorial identities', not a sieve; its output Theorem S (p.437) needs Type I at D = x^{1/2-eps} and Type II over y = x^{1/3-eps}, and concludes only sum_{p<=x} c_p << eps*pi(x) -- o(pi(x)), not a log-power saving. Its Type II coefficients are NOT arbitrary: '|alpha_m| <= omega(m), |beta_n| <= 1 ... and, in our case, beta_n will be supported on primes' (p.437). The arbitrary 1-bounded version, Type I at X^{1/2}(log X)^{-C} and Type II to X^{3/8}, is Green-Sawhney's strengthening (their Lemma 3.2), not DFI's.
claims.notes: Corrects an earlier `inferred` entry that attributed Green-Sawhney's strengthened hypotheses to DFI. Obtained from the author's own scan at math.ucla.edu/~wdduke/preprints/equidistribution.pdf, independently re-fetched and verified byte-identical.
claims.citation: Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec, Ann. of Math. 141 (1995), Theorem S and coefficient class p.437, Prop. 2 p.426; Green-Sawhney arXiv:2410.04189v3 Lemma 3.2 p.9

claims.statement: x^2+1 meets DFI's Type I hypothesis, so DFI's sieve applies to it.
claims.notes: Refuted on reading DFI directly. Theorem S is normalised to x, and A = {x+i} has mass x^{1/2} inside norm bound x, so applied verbatim the hypotheses hold trivially and the conclusion is weaker than the trivial bound -- vacuous, not satisfied. What survives is narrower and is filed as dfi-lemma2-is-scale-free.

claims.statement: x^2+1 fails DFI's arbitrary-coefficient Type II hypothesis outright: worst-case theta = 1.000, 0.999, 0.999 across N(m) in [10,100), [100,1000), [1000,1682) at X = 2e4. With beta = mu the same ranges give 0.627, 0.775, 0.825.
claims.notes: Exact integer computation over the stated finite range; settles that range completely and implies nothing asymptotic.

claims.statement: Green-Sawhney prove an asymptotic for primes p^2+nq^2 with p,q prime, n = 0 or 4 mod 6; at n=4 this settles Friedlander-Iwaniec's Gaussian Primes Conjecture. Their sequence has alpha = 1 and is not thin by FI's own criterion.
claims.citation: Green-Sawhney, Primes of the form p^2+nq^2, arXiv:2410.04189v3 Theorem 1.1 p.1 and p.2; FI Conjecture 1.1, arXiv:1811.05507v1 p.3

claims.statement: Two sieves break parity below x^{2/3}: Xiannan Li unconditionally, to exponential density 2/3 - gamma/3 for gamma < 5/67 (approx x^{0.6418}), and Merikoski conditionally on exceptional characters at 5/8. Neither reaches x^{1/2}.
claims.citation: Li, as reported with Maynard ICM survey Question 21; Merikoski arXiv:2108.01355
claims.notes: Quoted via subagent extraction with verbatim checks by an adversarial reviewer; the papers were not read in this repo.

claims.statement: Ford-Maynard Theorem 4.16 gives C^-(gamma,theta,nu) = 0 whenever gamma < 1/2 and gamma not in [theta,theta+nu]; Theorem 2.4 gives C^-(P_eps) = 0 at gamma = 1/2 with eps losses, remarking that 'one cannot hope to obtain non-trivial lower bounds on primes without some additional assumptions'. The escape named is divisor-bounded weights. This repo initially placed x^2+1 at gamma = 1/2 exactly; see x2plus1-sits-below-gamma-half, which corrects that to gamma = 1/2 - eps.
claims.citation: Ford-Maynard, On the theory of prime producing sieves, arXiv:2407.14368, Thm 2.4 p.6 and Thm 4.16 p.17
claims.notes: The gamma = 1/2 reading was wrong, and so was the correction to it: see fm-no-admissible-theta-at-density-half. Theorem 2.4 is quoted correctly here but does not apply to this sequence -- its hypothesis P in A*_2 requires nu >= 1/3 or theta + nu = 1/2, and Note F gives nu = 0. Its role on FM p.6 is the opposite of the use this repo made of it: the divisor-bounded repair of Theorem 2.4 is what rescues Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec.

claims.statement: Merikoski proves infinitude of primes a^2+b^2 with b in B for |B cap [0,Y]| >> Y^{1-delta}, without using ASP. His A(X) ~ X^{1/2}|B| = X^{1-delta}, so alpha ~ 1-delta; his large sieve needs N << X^{-eta}|B|, so |B| = 1 empties the Type II range at any delta.
claims.citation: Merikoski, On Gaussian primes in sparse sets, arXiv:2302.11331v3, Thms 1.1-1.3; Compositio Math. 161 (2025), 181-243

claims.statement: Ford-Maynard (arXiv:2407.14368) restates or relaxes FI's hypothesis (R1).
claims.notes: Conjectured by this repo as 'the likeliest place for a restated or relaxed (R1)'. Refuted: the paper never cites ASP, never states (R1) or (B1)-(B3), and never mentions gamma(n,C).

claims.statement: No sector equidistribution result, however narrow, bears on the line Im z = 1, because sectors are two-dimensional and the line is not.
claims.notes: Asserted in Note A, then refuted: a sector anchored at arg = 0 is a horizontal strip, and Harman-Lewis harvest exactly that to get primes m^2+n^2 with n < p^0.119. The line is the width ~X^{-1/2} limit of the family, and an asymptotic there would prove Landau's fourth problem.

claims.statement: The line Im z = 1 is the width ~X^{-1/2} limit of the narrow-sector family. Unconditional asymptotics reach width X^{-3/10+eps} (Ricci), GRH reaches X^{-1/2+eps} for individual sectors, and Harman-Lewis get a lower bound at width X^{-0.381}.
claims.citation: Huang-Liu-Rudnick, arXiv:1903.04005v1 sec.1; Harman-Lewis, Mathematika 48 (2001), 119-135
claims.notes: Ricci's thesis (Univ. Michigan 1976) is unpublished; the X^{-3/10+eps} figure is second-hand from three agreeing restatements.

claims.statement: For fixed m, {n : mn in A} is the arithmetic progression n_0 + Z*conj(m), because Im(mn)=1 is a line whose homogeneous solutions are n = t*conj(m).
mu of the Gaussian ideal (x+i) equals mu(x^2+1) as an integer, since each rational prime dividing x^2+1 contributes exactly one prime ideal with the same exponent.

Up to the non-squarefree correction, the Type II sum equals sum_q |sum_{x<=X, x==r_q mod q} mu(x^2+1)| -- a Bombieri-Vinogradov statement for mu(x^2+1) in arithmetic progressions, at moduli up to X^{3/4} for a sequence of X terms.
claims.notes: The X^{3/4} range comes from DFI's Type II window, which this repo knows at two removes; if that window differs, the level changes.

claims.statement: The per-progression saving rho = S/(pairs*sqrt(n)), n the actual mean progression length, is flat in X at fixed M band: fitted rho ~ (log X)^c gives c = -0.057 with a band-phase spread of 0.19 over X = 1e4..1e7, against an iid null returning -0.002 and an injected (log X)^{-1/2} recovered as -0.482. So the law is sqrt(MX) with no log-power correction, to a resolution of |c| <~ 0.2.
claims.notes: Cross-checked against all admissible moduli at X <= 1e5: rho = 0.636-0.667 vs 0.64-0.73 for prime moduli, so the restriction does not distort the level. It cannot check the exponent -- half a decade is too short to fit one. Fitted at fixed M band, not fixed u -- at fixed u the finite-n dependence of rho confounds the log-power and the fit scatters from -0.31 to +0.13. An earlier run normalised by the nominal band length and reported rho ~ 0.655; corrected to ~0.72, which leaves the fitted c unchanged. Shuffle and iid controls agree with the actual value to 1-2%, so mu shows no detectable structure along these progressions.

claims.statement: At X = 1e6, rho computed on the actual mu(x^2+1) agrees to within 1-2% with both a shuffled control (same values, random order) and a synthetic iid +-1/0 control at the same density, in every M band tested.
claims.notes: A negative result: no obstruction is visible in the correlation structure. It does NOT say mu is random, and truth is not provability -- the parity barrier is about the latter. Exact computation at one X.

claims.statement: DFI's Lemma 2 (p.436) assumes only (27) sum_{n==0(d)}|c_n| <= gamma(d)X with gamma submultiplicative and (29) gamma(p) <= c/p, so it applies to a thin sequence with gamma(d) = rho(d)/d and X ~ x^{1/2}. The Type I and Type II hypotheses must then be re-normalised to X = |A|, demanding cancellation of size |A|(log)^{-B}.
claims.citation: Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec, Ann. of Math. 141 (1995), Lemma 2 p.436, conditions (27) and (29)
claims.notes: Neither DFI nor Green-Sawhney writes the thin-sequence version down. The re-normalised level is where Note F's C4-free obstruction bites, and is the first place the repo's obstruction and the literature's machinery are in the same normalisation.

claims.statement: DFI's equidistribution theorem is for f(X) = aX^2+2bX+c with D = ac-b^2 > 0; a=1,b=0,c=1 gives D=1, so nu^2+1 == 0 (mod p) is literally covered. Their rho_h(n) = sum_{f(nu)==0 (n)} e(h nu/n) is the Weyl sum over this repo's residues r_d. Proposition 1 (p.425) bounds L_d(M) = sum_{M<m<=2M} rho_h(dm) << (h,d)^{1/20}(d/M)^{1/20}M^{1+eps}, uniformly in d up to d ~ M.
claims.citation: Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec, Ann. of Math. 141 (1995), Theorem p.424, Proposition 1 p.425, Proposition 2 p.426
claims.notes: Directly about this repo's admissible-ideal residues, and Note J reduces the Type II input to a statement about exactly these residues in progressions. BUT Proposition 1 bounds a SIGNED sum over m, and exp07 shows the difficulty is entirely in the absolute values -- so it is the right object in the wrong norm. Downgraded from 'sharpest open question' accordingly; it could still be an ingredient in an argument that handles the |.| by other means.

claims.statement: With no arbitrary-coefficient Type II range (nu = 0 in Ford-Maynard's sense, which Note F proves for this sequence), the Type I/II framework returns C^- = 0 by Selberg's example: 'whenever nu = 0, there are examples of a_n with b_n = 1 for all n which satisfy (I) for arbitrary gamma < 1 but with sum_p a_p = 0'. Ford-Maynard Theorem 2.1 is the quantitative version.
claims.citation: Ford-Maynard, arXiv:2407.14368v1, p.2 (Selberg [28]) and Theorem 2.1 p.3
claims.notes: C^- = 0 is a statement about what these axioms can prove -- there exists an admissible sequence with no primes -- NOT about whether x^2+1 is prime infinitely often. Do not conflate.

claims.statement: Ford-Maynard's (I) demands a log-power saving at level exactly x^gamma. Note B gives Type I for D = o(x^{1/2}) and failing at x^{1/2}, so x^2+1 is at gamma = 1/2 - eps for every eps, never gamma = 1/2 -- i.e. inside the P_eps regime that their Theorems 2.4 and 4.16 kill, not the gamma = 1/2 case where they assert C^{+-} = 1.
claims.citation: Ford-Maynard, arXiv:2407.14368v1, hypothesis (I) p.2, Theorem 2.4 p.6, Theorem 4.16 p.17
claims.notes: Refuted on the third reading of arXiv:2407.14368v1, for the attribution rather than the placement. Theorem 2.4's hypothesis is P in A*_2 = {(1/2,0,nu) : 1/3 <= nu < 1/2} union {(1/2,theta,1/2-theta) : 0 <= theta <= 1/3} (p.6); this sequence has nu = 0 and is in neither component, so Theorem 2.4 never applied. Theorem 4.16 does apply on the strict reading gamma < 1/2. But the gamma = 1/2 vs 1/2 - eps distinction was never load-bearing: FM's Table 1 caption reads 'epsilons omitted', so by that standard every entry including Friedlander-Iwaniec's x^{3/4-5eps} sits at gamma = level - eps. The conclusion C^- = 0 survives by Selberg / Theorem 2.1, which turn on nu = 0 and not on gamma at all.

claims.statement: Divisor-boundedness does not exempt x^2+1: Ford-Maynard Theorem 2.7(c) gives C^-(1/2,0,nu) = 0 = C^-_bd(1/2,0,nu) at nu = 0.1616, and C^-_bd(1/2,0,3/19) = 0. The divisor-bounded escape buys nothing once nu is small, whatever the density.
claims.citation: Ford-Maynard, arXiv:2407.14368v1, Theorem 2.7(c) p.8
claims.notes: Answers the [VERIFY] this repo carried as 'the sharpest live question': the indicator weight IS divisor-bounded, and it does not help.

claims.statement: The repo's beta = mu cancellation is arithmetic information not expressible as Ford-Maynard's (I)/(II) with arbitrary coefficients -- new ONLY because it holds on ranges where the arbitrary-coefficient hypothesis fails outright, which by Note F is every range. Ford-Maynard expect specialised-coefficient results to upgrade to full ones (footnote 1, p.3); Note F proves that here they cannot.
claims.notes: Inferred, not quoted: Ford-Maynard never discuss x^2+1 and the paper contains zero occurrences of 'Landau', 'x2+1', 'Gaussian' or 'quadratic polynomial'. A mu-restricted Type II is WEAKER than the arbitrary-coefficient one at the same range, so restricting coefficients is not per se an escape; the argument only works in the narrow form stated. An earlier version of this claim rested on a truncated quotation that omitted 'although often the methods generalize to give (II)'.

claims.statement: The Type II difficulty for x^2+1 is entirely in the absolute values. At X = 3e6 the signed sum |sum_q sum_{x==r_q (q)} mu(x^2+1)| is 0.4-1.9% of the absolute-value sum sum_q |...|, and is itself below sqrt(terms). Taking |.| per modulus IS taking the sup over signs, i.e. an arbitrary outer coefficient, which is exactly what Note F's C4-free lemma proves the sequence cannot support.
claims.notes: A measurement of Note F rather than a restatement of it: the two notes describe one obstruction from two sides. Exact computation at one X. Consequence: DFI's Proposition 1 bounds a SIGNED sum over the same residues, so it is the right object in the wrong norm -- see dfi-equidistribution-covers-nu2plus1.

claims.statement: DFI's proof is spectral and reaches the roots of nu^2+1 == 0 directly, via Poincare series and the spectral expansion in Maass cusp forms and Eisenstein series -- 'roots of the congruence to the spectrum of the Laplacian without passing through Kloosterman sums along the way'. Its output is Proposition 1, a bound on the SIGNED sum L_d(M). DFI also state that Selberg's eigenvalue conjecture would give sharper estimates but 'the same range of uniformity', which is the axis this repo needs.
claims.citation: Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec, Ann. of Math. 141 (1995), pp.427 and 429 (Poincare series, sec.3)
claims.notes: Corrects Note G, which had assumed the spectral route was inapplicable because dispersion produces no Kloosterman sums here. True of dispersion, false of spectral methods. But spectral is not an independent option: it is the engine behind Prop 1, so it inherits the wrong-norm problem measured in exp07.

claims.statement: Merikoski (2022) proves sum_{p<=X} #{p = a^2+(b^2+1)^2} asymptotic to X^{3/4}/log X -- a lower bound of the correct order, NOT an asymptotic formula. Type I to D <= X^{3/4-eta'} (Prop. 4); Type II for X^{1/4+eta} << N << X^{1/3-eta} (Prop. 12), against Friedlander-Iwaniec's X^{1/4+eta} << N << X^{1/2-eta}. Coefficients: alpha(m) bounded and arbitrary, beta(n) bounded with the Siegel-Walfisz property (4.1), reduced to Siegel-Walfisz with main term 0 (4.2) by a device of Heath-Brown.
claims.citation: Merikoski, The polynomials X^2+(Y^2+1)^2 and X^2+(Y^3+Z^3)^2 also capture their primes, arXiv:2112.03617v2, Thm 1 p.2, Prop. 4 p.7, (4.1) p.14, Prop. 12 p.15, Prop. 13 p.16
claims.notes: The fourth published sequence with a known outcome. Its density is identical to a^2+b^4 by construction, so it varies structure while holding density fixed. Merikoski p.6 defines rho_1(d) = #{nu (d) : nu^2+1 = 0 (d)}, which is this repo's rho.

claims.statement: The +1 desingularises the Type II curve and that cuts both ways. Main term: for a != 0,1 the homogenisation (1-a)x_0^2 + x_1^2 - a x_2^2 is non-singular, so Weil gives eps_p(a) << p^{1/2} and the divisor sum truncates at d <= log^{2C}X -- 'having (b^2+1)^2 rather than b^4 turns out to be a friend rather than an enemy'. Error term: on the non-singular curve S(a,h1,h2;Delta) << |Delta|^{1/2+eps} << N^{1/2+eps}, 'sufficient provided that N << X^{1/3-eta}', where FI's singular curve gives S_FI << N^eps, 'which is why for a^2+b^4 one can handle the Type II sums up to N << X^{1/2-eta}'.
claims.citation: Merikoski, The polynomials X^2+(Y^2+1)^2 and X^2+(Y^3+Z^3)^2 also capture their primes, arXiv:2112.03617v2, pp. 4-5 and Section 5 p.16
claims.notes: Both halves of the trade run through the Poisson sum over b1, b2 with B1,B2 << X^{1/4}. Neither survives B = 1. So this is not a route for x^2+1; it is the mechanism that explains why kappa alone cannot predict the Type II range.

claims.statement: At Q = 10^7, a^2+b^4 and a^2+(b^2+1)^2 agree in |A| to 0.02%, in kappa to 0.04% (2368.2 vs 2367.2) and in max-over-splits min(D_m,d_n) to 2.7% (41.22 vs 40.12), and both have 4-cycles. The literature separates them by 1/6 in the Type II exponent and by asymptotic vs lower-bound. So kappa > 1 is necessary for a usable Type II range and is not sufficient.
claims.notes: The first control in this repo that varies structure at fixed density; every earlier comparison varied both together. Downgrades how much weight Notes D and F may put on kappa. The direction Note F actually uses -- kappa = 1 implies a forest implies no main term -- is unaffected.

claims.statement: For A = {a + f(b)i} with a << Q^{1/2} and b << B, |A| ~ Q^{1/2}B so kappa = |A|^2/Q = B^2 identically, and sqrt(kappa) = B is the range of the Poisson summation variables in the Type II reduction (Merikoski p.4: 'for any B_1, B_2 << X^{1/4}' at alpha = 3/4). For x^2+1, B = 1: Poisson summation over one point is the identity, so there is no main term to evaluate and no exponential sum to bound.
claims.notes: kappa = B^2 is arithmetic. The identification of B with the Poisson range is this repo's reading of Merikoski p.4 and is not stated anywhere in the literature; that is the inferred step. It is also only checked for sequences of the form a + f(b)i.

claims.statement: Ford-Maynard name Note F's counting function as the barrier: 'Showing one can take theta + nu >= 1 - 2c is closely related to estimating #{n : nm_1, nm_2 in J} with an error term better than O(1) on average over m_1, m_2 ~ x^{1-2c+eps} (i.e. to show bilinear cancellation in the error term), which is typically very difficult outside of special situations.' That is G(n_1,n_2) with the variables named the other way.
claims.citation: Ford-Maynard, On the theory of prime producing sieves, arXiv:2407.14368v1, footnote 2 p.7
claims.notes: External evidence that Note F measures the right object; Note F was derived from the Z[i] structure, not read out of a paper. Where they say 'typically very difficult', Note F proves the count is 0 or 1, so the error term IS O(1) and no averaging helps.

claims.statement: Ford-Maynard's Table 1, caption 'Examples from the literature (epsilons omitted)', lists eight successful (gamma, theta, nu). Every one has nu > 0. The smallest is Merikoski Thm 1 at (3/4, 1/4, 1/12); Friedlander-Iwaniec are at (3/4, 1/4, 1/2) and Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec at (1/2, 0, 1/3). So gamma = 1/2 is not fatal in itself -- with nu = 1/3 and divisor-bounded weights it works, and FM p.6 says so: 'This was exploited in Duke-Friedlander-Iwaniec [7] in the case theta = 0, nu = 1/3'.
claims.citation: Ford-Maynard, On the theory of prime producing sieves, arXiv:2407.14368v1, Table 1 p.3 and p.6
claims.notes: nu = 1/12 suffices for a lower bound via Harman's sieve, so the bar is not a wide arbitrary-coefficient Type II range; it is nu > 0. Note F gives nu = 0 here.

claims.statement: x^2+1 has no admissible Ford-Maynard parameter triple. For J of size x^{1-c}, FM p.7: 'one can only hope for (I) to hold for gamma < 1 - c and (II) for theta > c'; and (1.1) p.1 requires 0 <= theta < 1/2. At density x^{1/2}, c = 1/2, so (II) needs theta > 1/2 and (1.1) needs theta < 1/2. Computed by x2plus1.exponents.ford_maynard_theta, which raises at alpha = 1/2 and returns [1/4,1/2) at alpha = 3/4 and [1/3,1/2) at alpha = 2/3.
claims.notes: The deduction is the repo's; FM state the two ingredients but never draw the conclusion for c >= 1/2, and 'one can only hope' is an informal remark inside their discussion of the family P_theta, not a theorem. What it replaces is the gamma = 1/2 - eps argument, which turned on a distinction FM's own Table 1 caption discards. Also worth noting: their 'gamma < 1 - c' is Note B's ceiling, reached independently.
